title: The X-Files: I Want to Believe
full_review:
"The X-Files: I Want to Believe" (Fox), which reaches theaters six years after the last episode of the television series aired, proves a grim investigative drama with an unlikely and somewhat ghoulish plotline.

Ex-FBI agents Dana Scully (Gillian Anderson), and Fox Mulder (David Duchovny), long the bureau's go-to pair for all things paranormal, have left alien-hunting behind, she by choice, he by necessity. Scully is now a full-time doctor, while Mulder is a fugitive from charges trumped up by his superiors to discredit him.

 

When current bureau official Dakota Whitney (Amanda Peet) asks the two to assist in a kidnapping investigation, it's understood that, if he surfaces, the case against Mulder will be dropped. But the request comes at a bad time for Scully.

She's been caring for Christian (Marco Niccoli), a courageous young boy dying of a rare disease, and her concern for him has become as much personal as professional. Despite this, she not only agrees to help, but travels to Mulder's remote hideout and convinces him to do the same.

The hunt is being guided by -- of all people -- a Catholic priest, Father Joseph Crissman (Billy Connolly), both a convicted pedophile and a purported psychic. Appalled by Father Joe's crimes, Scully insists he's a fake, but Mulder is more open-minded, recognizing that the seedy clergyman may have a chance for redemption.

Scully, meanwhile, clashes with another man of the cloth. Respectable but hidebound hospital director Father Ybarra (Adam Godley) is determined to ship her terminal patient off to a hospice, rather than allow Scully to attempt an experimental course of treatment.

 

Director Chris Carter, co-writing with TV collaborator Frank Spotnitz, has created a rather ordinary second film derived from their popular 1993-2002 small-screen series. The central conflict between Duchovny's charismatic idealism and Anderson's show-me cynicism is weakened by a slow, derivative story.

The script raises issues of medical ethics, faith and forgiveness. Is Scully right to insist on every possible remedy for the dying child? Does her persistence in keeping him alive merely demonstrate a lack of faith? Is forgiveness possible even for a Father Joseph? But, these themes are treated only superficially.

 

Inconsistencies abound. For example, how does Scully so easily shuttle back and forth between the operating table and the various crime scenes?

The film contains action violence, surgical gore including severed limbs and body parts, an implied nonmarital relationship, sexual references, occasional crude and crass language and a profanity. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
